params.question: Based on the epidemiological data presented, which statement best explains why iron deficiency anaemia is described as an 'epidemic' in India?

answers.text: It has a high case fatality rate among hospitalised patients

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IDA rarely kills acutely. Its burden is chronic — impairing productivity, cognitive development, and maternal outcomes over years, not through acute mortality.

answers.text: It affects more than half of women of reproductive age and two-thirds of young children

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NFHS-5 reports 57% of women aged 15–49 and 67% of children aged 6–59 months are anaemic, with iron deficiency as the primary driver — prevalence figures that justify the term 'epidemic.'

answers.text: It is primarily caused by genetic haemoglobin disorders prevalent in the Indian population

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thalassaemia and other haemoglobinopathies exist in India, but the dominant cause of anaemia in women and children is nutritional iron deficiency, not inherited haemoglobin disorders.

answers.text: It has been rising sharply due to rapid urbanisation since 2010

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration does not attribute the epidemic to recent urbanisation. The high prevalence reflects longstanding structural factors — vegetarian diets, reproductive demands, and parasitic infections.

overallFeedback.feedback: NFHS-5 found 57% of women aged 15–49 and 67% of children aged 6–59 months are anaemic, largely from iron deficiency. This extraordinary prevalence is what defines the epidemic.
Correct. The sheer prevalence — over half of reproductive-age women and two-thirds of young children — makes iron deficiency anaemia a public health epidemic in India.

interactions.label: Why does the video emphasise that gastrointestinal blood loss must be urgently i

params.question: Why does the video emphasise that gastrointestinal blood loss must be urgently investigated in adult males and post-menopausal women with unexplained iron deficiency anaemia?

answers.text: Because dietary iron deficiency is uncommon in patients with unrestricted diets, making other causes unlikely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While dietary deficiency may be less likely in these groups, this does not explain the urgency. The narration highlights a specific danger that makes investigation of GI blood loss a priority.

answers.text: Because Helicobacter pylori infection is more prevalent in older adults and must be treated first

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: H. pylori can impair iron absorption, but it is not the reason the video singles out GI blood loss for urgent investigation. The concern is a more serious underlying pathology.

answers.text: Because iron absorption naturally declines after menopause, making malabsorption the default diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Menopause does not inherently impair iron absorption. The urgency arises not from an absorption defect but from the risk that chronic GI blood loss may have a dangerous cause.

answers.text: Because gastrointestinal bleeding in these demographics may indicate an underlying malignancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration explicitly states that any adult male or post-menopausal woman with unexplained IDA must have gastrointestinal malignancy excluded first. This makes blood loss the most clinically urgent category to investigate.

overallFeedback.feedback: The narration stresses that any adult male or post-menopausal woman with unexplained IDA must have gastrointestinal malignancy excluded. This cancer risk is why blood loss demands urgent investigation.
Correct. In adult males and post-menopausal women, gastrointestinal blood loss may signal a malignancy — the reason it must be investigated urgently before considering other causes.

interactions.label: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a triad associated with iron deficiency anaemia. Why

params.question: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a triad associated with iron deficiency anaemia. Why is recognising this syndrome clinically important?

answers.text: It indicates that the anaemia will not respond to oral iron therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Plummer-Vinson syndrome does not predict treatment refractoriness. Its significance lies in a structural and oncological risk described in the narration.

answers.text: It confirms coeliac disease as the underlying cause of iron deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is unrelated to coeliac disease. The triad consists of iron deficiency anaemia, post-cricoid dysphagia, and oesophageal webs — a distinct clinical entity.

answers.text: It carries a 10 to 15 percent risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the pharynx or upper oesophagus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration identifies Plummer-Vinson syndrome as premalignant. The triad of IDA, post-cricoid dysphagia, and oesophageal webs carries a 10–15% risk of squamous cell carcinoma, making active follow-up mandatory.

answers.text: It predicts irreversible neurological damage from impaired myelination

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Irreversible cognitive impairment from impaired myelination is a concern in paediatric iron deficiency, not in Plummer-Vinson syndrome, which involves mucosal and structural changes in the upper aerodigestive tract.

overallFeedback.feedback: The narration describes Plummer-Vinson syndrome (IDA + post-cricoid dysphagia + oesophageal webs) as premalignant, carrying a 10–15% risk of pharyngeal or upper oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
Correct. Plummer-Vinson syndrome is premalignant — the 10–15% cancer risk makes recognition and follow-up essential.

params.question: The video states that oral iron therapy should continue even after haemoglobin normalises. What is the reason for this recommendation?

answers.text: To replenish the body's depleted iron stores, which recover more slowly than haemoglobin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haemoglobin normalises before body iron stores are fully replenished. The 3–6 month continuation ensures that ferritin and tissue iron reserves are restored, preventing early relapse.

answers.text: To prevent rebound haemolysis that occurs when iron supplements are stopped abruptly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Iron supplementation does not cause rebound haemolysis on discontinuation. The reason for continuing is that body iron stores need additional time to refill after haemoglobin reaches normal levels.

answers.text: To allow the reticulocyte count to return to baseline before stopping therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Reticulocytosis is a transient early response (days 3–5) that resolves on its own. It is not the reason for prolonged therapy — the concern is incomplete store replenishment.

answers.text: To ensure that the absorbed iron is converted into the storage form rather than haemoglobin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Iron distribution between haemoglobin and stores is regulated physiologically, not by treatment duration. The real issue is that stores lag behind haemoglobin recovery and need continued supplementation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Stopping iron at haemoglobin normalisation is a common error. The narration stresses 3–6 months of continued therapy because body iron stores remain depleted even after haemoglobin reaches normal levels.
Correct. Body iron stores recover more slowly than haemoglobin. Continuing oral iron for 3–6 months after normalisation prevents relapse by fully replenishing depleted reserves.
